title: Microsoft almost made a Surface phone we actually wanted

body: TL;DR Microsoft reportedly had plans for a Surface-branded Windows Phone years before the Surface Duo, with a 2013-2014 prototype recently revealed. The mysterious phone featured a 720p display, physical navigation buttons, a silver Surface-like chassis, and Windows Phone 8.1. The Nokia acquisition may have killed the project, while Microsoft’s eventual Surface Duo took a very different dual-screen approach that came with plenty of compromises. Microsoft’s Surface Duo and Surface Duo 2 were ambitious first attempts from a company that had little to no experience building smartphones all by itself. The Lumia phones did carry Microsoft’s software and branding, but those phones weren’t truly built just by Microsoft — they still carried a lot of Nokia’s DNA. 2020’s Surface Duo, arguably, was Microsoft’s first smartphone designed and developed as a true first-party Surface device on its own terms. And sometimes, you do everything right — from the writing to the performance to the release strategy to the promotional push — and you still end up just short of the ultimate goal. It focuses on agentic AI, with the ability to code, use tools, handle multi-step tasks, and recover from errors. The model is available now on Hugging Face, with support for popular local AI tools coming soon. Most modern, capable AI models rely on cloud computing to give you fast and reliable responses — your prompt and associated data has to leave your device, head to a server, get processed by the model in use, and then make its way back to you as a response. But we’ve also seen models taking an on-device approach, one that minimizes concerns related to cloud-based AI, but at the same time introducing their own limitations. A new model from Meta takes the latter approach, and it does so in a way that tackles some of on-device AI’s main constraints head on. With cloud-based AI, one of the biggest limitations is that models cannot run without an active internet connection. Models like Meta’s new Muse Glimmer that run totally on-device don’t face this limitation.

title: Anker SOLIX says most portable power stations waste up to 30% of their stored energy
summary: The company is publishing efficiency data it says the rest of the industry doesn't share.
body: Anker SOLIX has called out an entire industry over how it measures battery efficiency, and it’s using its own product to make the point. The company has published discharge efficiency data for its S Series portable power stations across a range of real-world loads, something it says makes it the first portable power brand to disclose this level of detail. Anker has also shared its testing methodology alongside the results. The issue, according to Anker, is how efficiency gets advertised in the first place. Most portable power brands quote a single efficiency figure, typically between 89 and 92%, measured near full load under ideal conditions. But that’s rarely how these devices actually get used. During a real outage, you’re more likely running a fridge, a CPAP machine, a router, and some lights, all of which draw under 300W, well below 15% of a typical 2,000W unit’s rated output. Anker says efficiency at those lighter loads commonly drops to 70 to 80%, meaning a meaningful chunk of stored energy never makes it to your devices.

body: Credit: Stephen Radochia / Android Authority TL;DR An AI agent found a vulnerability in a gym booking system and used it to book classes months earlier than the software normally allowed. What started as a pretty ordinary request to book a spot in a popular morning gym class turned into Australia’s first known autonomous cyber attack.

title: A Snapdragon-powered Pixel might sound amazing. Here’s why it’s a terrible idea
summary: Do you really wanna pay a lot more money for your Pixel flagship?
body: Credit: David Imel / Android Authority It’s been roughly five years since Google first dropped Snapdragon silicon in Pixel phones in favor of its Tensor processors. I think it’s fair to say this move has been a double-edged sword for the company. Sure, there’s been good everyday performance, capable on-device AI, and great camera capabilities. But the transition also brought modem issues, heating problems, and uncompetitive peak performance. This state of affairs has led enthusiasts to urge Google to return to Snapdragon silicon, and it seems like an intriguing idea at first. title: Before you buy another USB-C charger, make sure it has this critical (and hidden) spec
summary: Buying a USB-C charger is still harder than it should be.
body: Credit: Robert Triggs / Android Authority Buying the perfect USB-C charger may look simple at first, but the reality is full of potential gotchas. If you’ve ever reached for your cable only to find that your device is still charging hours later, you’re certainly not alone. In one sense, USB-C and USB Power Delivery were supposed to solve this mess. The universal connector and new regulations, such as those introduced in the EU, were designed to ensure that one charger could support everything. In some ways, that has been a success: USB-C can now be found on almost every phone, tablet, laptop, and more. However, the difference between something that technically works and something that works optimally can still be surprisingly wide.

body: TL;DR Android Authority has reviewed strings related to a new Pixel feature called Conversation Capture. Conversation Capture will record and transcribe audio, and with optional Gemini integration. We expect this feature will debut on the Pixel 11 series. One of Google’s best machine-learning enabled products has long been its Pixel-exclusive Recorder app, which makes searchable transcriptions of your recordings. Now, Google is integrating that basic concept deeper into the Android experience with a feature called Conversation Capture. Poking around the latest version of the Android System Intelligence app , we’ve seen a whole bunch of strings about Conversation Capture. Internally codenamed Auris, the feature sounds very similar to Google’s existing Recorder app, but built more deeply integrated with both Android and Gemini.
